name: Acceleration Structures and Traversal
text:
# Acceleration Structures and Traversal
## Overview
This family encompasses the algorithmic strategies for navigating volumetric data structures and the spatial metadata used to skip empty or occluded regions during ray casting [G]. It solves the problem of mapping continuous ray paths to discrete data elements while minimizing memory bandwidth and computation [G]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [GL-NeRF](803-gl-nerf.md) and [Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map](990-occlusion-clipping-with-orthogonal-opacity-map.md) by focusing on the topology of the data access path and explicit hierarchical culling rather than neural approximation or rasterized proxies [G].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism shared by all children is the determination of the sequence of data elements (voxels, cells, or bricks) intersected by a ray, and the retrieval of values from those elements [G]. This involves:
1. **Path Parameterization:** Representing the ray as $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ and computing intersection intervals $[t_{entry}, t_{exit}]$ with data boundaries [G].
2. **Coordinate Mapping:** Transforming the continuous ray parameter $t$ into discrete data indices (e.g., voxel coordinates, cell IDs, or brick IDs) [G].
3. **Data Retrieval:** Fetching the value at the mapped index from the appropriate memory structure (texture, buffer, or mesh) [G].

Mathematically, for a [uniform grid](#920-uniform-grid.md), this is often a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) step [G]. For irregular grids, it involves explicit boundary intersection tests [G]. For hierarchical data, it involves Level of Detail (LoD) selection and cache residency checks [G].

## Subtopics

### [Acceleration Structure Rebuild](3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md)
Discards the previous frame's [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structure and constructs a new one from scratch every frame for animated scenes [3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md]. It supports arbitrary, unrestricted animation types by avoiding the complexity and limitations of incremental or hierarchical update schemes [3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md]. It differs from siblings like [Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping](6289-adaptive-multi-step-empty-voxel-skipping.md) or [Temporal Coherence and Caching](6372-temporal-coherence-and-caching.md) by rejecting temporal reuse of the structure itself, relying instead on full reconstruction speed and parallel processing [3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md].

### [Traversal and Data Access](13739-traversal-and-data-access.md)
Covers the algorithmic strategies for moving a ray through a volume dataset and retrieving scalar values for [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [13739-traversal-and-data-access.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings like [GL-NeRF](803-gl-nerf.md) and [Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling](10063-space-skipping-and-empty-volume-culling.md) by focusing on the topology of the data access path and memory availability [13739-traversal-and-data-access.md].

### [LLO-based Ray-casting](16481-llo-based-ray-casting.md)
A volume rendering technique that accelerates [image-order rendering](#16-image-order-rendering.md) by utilizing a [Linear Level Octree (LLO)](#16467-linear-level-octree-llo.md) spatial data structure to skip empty space and facilitate early ray termination [16481-llo-based-ray-casting.md]. It differs from brute-force ray-casting by replacing uniform voxel traversal with [hierarchical octree traversal](#1587-octree-traversal.md), and from other acceleration structures by encoding the [octree](#18524-octree.md) in a linear array to optimize cache residency and memory access patterns [16481-llo-based-ray-casting.md].

### [Empty Space Skipping via Acceleration Structures](17387-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structures.md)
Accelerates volume rendering by identifying and bypassing transparent or empty regions of the volume data before expensive sampling and compositing occur [17387-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structures.md]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on geometric proxies [16346-progressive-ray-casting-for-volumetric-models-on-mobile-devi.md], this family constructs explicit hierarchical or grid-based metadata structures (e.g., octrees, BVHs, min/max grids) to determine ray visibility [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md]. It sets itself apart from [SparseLeap](5152-sparseleap.md) by typically using scalar min/max values or occupancy flags rather than rasterized segment lists, and from [Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping](8182-hierarchical-bounding-box-tree-for-empty-space-skipping.md) by employing fixed-grid [brick structures](#21349-brick-based-structures.md) or specific tree traversals rather than generic bounding box hierarchies [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md].

### Two-level Data Structures for Articulated Bodies
A structure for scenes with dynamic parts [S1, unofficial]. Uses a global grid/structure where articulated bodies (rigid parts) are inserted as elementary objects [S1, unofficial]. Each rigid part has its own local grid or data structure [S1, unofficial]. It is a technique for accelerating ray tracing in scenes with articulated bodies (rigid parts connected by joints) by separating static and dynamic components into different acceleration structures [S1, unofficial]. Implementation uses a separate grid or data structure for each self-contained rigid part of the articulated body [S1, unofficial]. It uses a global grid to store the individual parts as elementary objects [S1, unofficial]. When the figure moves, only update the global grid; the local structures for rigid parts do not need updating [S1, unofficial].

### Hash-based subvolume skipping
Approximate the hash table for a subtile by taking the union of the hash tables at the 4 surrounding corners and send it to the corresponding SPE [S2]. The SPE skips a sampling point if it belongs to an empty subvolume by checking the hash table [S2]. The hash key is computed as $key = (ranX \cdot x + ranY \cdot y + ranZ \cdot z) \pmod{PR}$ [S2]. Parameters: PR is a prime number equal to the hash table size; ranX, ranY, ranZ are random numbers strictly less than PR; x, y, z are the smallest coordinates of the subvolume [S2]. Pitfall: False positives are possible (an empty subvolume may be recognized as non-empty), but false negatives never occur [S2]. The false alarm rate can be significantly reduced by setting the hash table size large enough [S2].
